newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan sacks province govt, fearing mini states.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan sacks province govt, fearing mini states.

text.p: Pakistani president Farooq Leghari, moving to strengthen control over south-western regions ahead of national elections, sacked a provincial government on Friday, accusing it of encouraging notions of a "mini-state".
The move, the second such action in two days, came as former prime minister Benazir Bhutto, dismissed by Leghari on Tuesday, prepared to launch a campaign to recapture power.

The governor of the southwestern province of Baluchistan dissolved the local parliament and a coalition cabinet there on the president's orders. He accused sacked legislators of speaking against national unity in violation of Pakistan's constitution.

"Constitutional provisions also stand violated by the mischievous activities of some of the members of the coalition government to the extent that it gives an impression that efforts are afoot to create mini states within the state," a notice issued by governor Imranullah Khan said.
The remarks seemed aimed at nationalist groups seeking greater autonomy for their province.

The Baluchistan government of Chief Minister Zulfikar Ali Magsi ceased to exist after the dissolution of the 43-member provincial assembly, the state radio quoted a government notification issued in the provincial capital Quetta as saying.

The move in Pakistan's largest but least populated province, which borders Iran and Afghanistan, came a day after a similar action in the country's most industrialised region and Bhutto's home province of Sindh.

There was no immediate announcement of a new caretaker chief minister to replace Magsi, a tribal chief and a member of anti-Bhutto Pakistan Muslim League (PML) party, who headed a 31-member coalition government of various parties.
On Tuesday, Leghari dissolved the lower house of parliament. He sacked Bhutto on disputed charges of corruption and misrule and ordering fresh elections on February 3.
Political sources said the dissolution of assemblies in Pakistan's two other provinces -- Punjab and North West Frontier -- would be ordered at any time.

The grounds cited for the action in Baluchistan were similar to those given for sacking Bhutto and the Sindh government of her Pakistan People's Party (PPP), including corruption, misrule and violation of laws.
Most members of the Baluchistan cabinet had earlier spoken against a dissolution of the assembly and some said they would go to court if it were carried out.
Bhutto said on Thursday night she expected to file a legal challenge next week to Leghari's order toppling her government.
She promised to tour the country to whip up support for the PPP, now that the four-day-old caretaker government had lifted curbs on her movements.
"I am going to fight back," Bhutto told Reuters Television in an interview.
Bhutto was expected to meet advisers on Friday to discuss the court challenge to Leghari's trenchant order, which she called illegal and unconstitutional.
